content.title: This paper studies the problem of image classification models trained on dataset of long-tailed distribution that they are prone to be mis-calibrated and over-confident even with the state-of-the-art two-stage methods. The proposed label-aware smoothing and shifted batch normalization are very interesting ideas, and their efficacy in improving calibration and classification performance on long-tailed datasets has been proved in the extensive experimentation.
content.review:
Strengths
- The paper is well-written and the story is clear. 
- It gives a nice overview on related work especially on recently published methods for training classifiers on imbalanced datasets, calibration and regularization methods. 
- It explored the effect of mixup in the two-stage decoupling framework. The proposed label aware smoothing is an effective method for handling the different degrees of over-confidence for different classes. It’s also the first work to study the dataset bias or domain shift in two-stage resampling methods for long-tailed recognition. The findings provide good insights in building deep models for long-tailed image classification. The experiments are mostly thorough and detailed. 

Other comments:
- Mixup seems to contribute the most to the overall performance improvement, as we can observe from Table 2. However the efficacy of mixup has been studied in previous work, e.g. Thulasidasan et al. (2019), which found that networks trained with mixup are better calibrated. Table 4 also shows that mixup can improve other state-of-the-art methods which achieve performance close to the proposed MiSLAS.
- Does the proposed method use the same hyperparameters as the other two-stage methods like cRT or LWS?
- When first referring to cRT and LWS, it’s better to include their full names as well.
- Please define N_j before using it in Figure 2’s caption firstly.
- The paper did experiments on different IFs, but doesn’t have much discussion on how the proposed method’s performance is related to IF. Adding more detailed analysis on this will also be useful.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer Feedback
content.comment:
We would like to thank Reviewer 1’s support and constructive comments. 

Q1: Mixup seems to contribute the most to the overall performance improvement.

A1: For the improvement of test accuracy, mixup seems to contribute the most. However, **when we consider the calibration performance, the proposed label-aware smoothing contributes the most.** Here are the detailed results of test accuracy and calibration performance of Table 2 in the ablation study part (Accuracy[%]/ECE) :


\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}
\\hline
  & \text{Module}& & & \text{CIFAR-100-LT} \\\\
\\hline
\\hline
\text{MU}  & \text{SL}  & \text{LAS}  &  \text{IF=100}&\text{IF=50}& \text{IF=10} \\\\
\\hline
\text{w/o}  & \text{w/o}  & \text{w/o}  &  \text{41.2/0.36}&\text{46.0/0.34}& \text{58.5/0.27} \\\\
\text{w}  & \text{w/o}  & \text{w/o}  &  \text{44.2/0.22}&\text{50.6/0.18}& \text{62.2/0.14} \\\\
\text{w}  & \text{w}  & \text{w/o}  &  \text{45.3/0.22}&\text{51.4/0.19}& \text{62.8/0.13} \\\\
\text{w}  & \text{w}  & \text{w}  &  \text{47.0/0.04}&\text{52.3/0.05}& \text{63.0/0.04} \\\\
\\hline
\end{array}

We have already cited the work, Thulasidasan et al. (2019), please refer to the related works part of our paper. Our paper is highly motivated by this work. We find that the calibration of the network trained on an imbalanced dataset becomes worse. Thus, we apply mixup to relieve over-confidence and improve representation learning in Stage-1.

Q2: Does the proposed method use the same hyperparameters as the other two-stage methods like cRT or LWS?

A2: Yes. For a fair comparison, we use the same hyperparameters setting for training and evaluation when we compare MiSLAS with cRT or LWS.

Q3: More discussion about the proposed method’s performance with different IF.

A3: Based on the previous research, the accuracy performances of all long-tailed models will increase if we apply a smaller IF value because the imbalance degree of the dataset becomes weaker. However, the gain of test accuracy will be limited if the IF value is small enough. According to our experiment results,  we observe that MiSLAS also follows this trend. Additionally,  when IF decreasing and the dataset distribution becomes more balanced, all models tend to have a lower ECE. Further Reducing ECE and improving calibration become more and more difficult at the same time.

Overall, we thank the reviewer again for the other valuable comments to improve the quality of the paper.

content.title: This paper is aimed at long-tailed recognition. It finds that cRT and LWS in Decoupling suffer over-confidence and are prone to miscralibrated. It uses mixup to remedy this problem and proposes a label-aware smoothing method to improve classifier. Besides these, it is the first to note the dataset bias between different sampling strategies in 2 stages and proposes BN shifting to solve it.
content.review:
The proposed method has large limitation as it fully based on cRT and LWS. The novelty and original work are unadequate since the most contribution is adding mixup to stage 1 and re-weighting to stage 2. The performance improvement is small.
Pros:
1. The motivation and solution are clear and easy to unstand.
2. The view of over-confidence is interesting and novel.
3. The experiment and analysis are adequate
3. The paper finds that different sampling strategies make the data distribution different and proposes to use BN shifting to solve this problem.
Cons:
1. In 3.1, the paper judges that mixup damages the classifier but data in tabel 1 doesn’t reflect this problem.
2. The proposed label-aware smoothing is in fact a re-weighting technique which gives bigger loss to tail class and smaller loss to head class. Howerver, in the part of analyzing the reliability diagrams, the paper only covers cRT and LWS which are not re-weighting methods.
3. The proposed method is fully based on Decoupling cRT and LWS, which has high limitation.
4. The performance improvement on Imagenet_LT is small, which is only 1% higher than cRT+mixup and 0.7% higher than LWS+mixup.
5. The novelty and originality are not enough. It is virtually adding mixup to stage 1 and re-weighting to stage 2.
6. An error: the cRT retrain the classifier from scratch rather than finetuning.
7. How to get the equivalent (2) is unclear.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

display_title: Replies on some critical misunderstandings of our contribution

content.title: Replies on some critical misunderstandings of our contribution
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate the valuable review. We want to, however, rebut some criticisms that are critical to understanding our contribution:

**1. Novelty and difference to re-weight methods**

We would like to highlight that our objective is **improving calibration.** The proposed label-aware smoothing is quite different from the re-weight methods. Concretely, label-aware smoothing changes the hard label to a soft version of the label based on the label distribution (see Eqn. (1), otherwise case: $\boldsymbol{q}_i=\frac{f(N_y)}{K-1}, i \neq y$). While re-weight methods don't contain such critical transformation and just set the values to zero in the otherwise case: $\boldsymbol{q}_i=0, i \neq y$. 

**It is the label transformation involved in MiSLAS that improves calibration and relieves the over-confidence phenomenon rather than the re-weight operation helps to improve calibration.** Furthermore, due to the transformation of labels, the optimal solution of ${\boldsymbol{w}_i^*}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ becomes Eqn. (2) (proof of a simple vision of label-aware smoothing, i.e., label smoothing, please refer https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.01187). By contrast, the optimal solution of re-weight methods is just the same as it of cross-entropy, i.e., ${{\boldsymbol{w}_i^*}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}=\inf}$, which cannot properly change the predicted distribution and leads to over-confidence. Last but not least, based on our experiments of LT CIFAR-100 with imbalanced factor (IF) 100, 50, and 10, using the re-weight method (Effective number, refer https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.05555) in Stage-2 **degrades both the performance and calibration.** (lower accuracy result and larger expected calibration error)


\begin{array}{l|ccc}
\\hline
\text{Metric}  & \text{IF=100}&\text{IF=50}& \text{IF=10} \\\\
\\hline
\\hline
\text{Re-weight (Effective number)}  & 44.3\\%/0.20   & 50.5\\%/0.19    & 62.5\\%/0.13 \\\\
\text{Label-aware smoothing}  & 47.0\\%/0.04& 52.3\\%/0.05   & 63.2\\%/0.04   \\\\
\\hline
\end{array}

**2. Limitation and improvement of performance**

Actually, our model is a general two-stage method rather than a model based on the decoupling cRT and LWS. **Our MiSLAS can be applied to any two-stage methods with consistent performance gains.** For example, we conduct experiments on LT CIFAR-100 with imbalanced factor 100. The original two-stage method DRS (please refer https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07413) achieves accuracy at 40.4%. By comparison, DRS combining with our model for two stages can obtain accuracy at 45.1% further.

The baselines (cRT+mixup and LWS+mixup) in our experiments part are powerful enough that, to the best of our knowledge, **all previous methods even suffer great difficulties in exceeding the baseline of cRT+mixup.** However, the proposed model can distinctly surpass this baseline by 3.0% on LT CIFAR-10, 1.9% on LT CIFAR-100, 1.4% on iNaturalist, and 2.1% on Places-LT, respectively. We also mention in the last paragraph of Section 3.2 that cRT learns a new classifier weight in Stage-2.

Finally, our conceptual novelty of improving calibration and relieving dataset bias in two-stage methods has been echoed by both Reviewer 1 & 2. We hope their comments can clarify further.

display_title: Interesting paper with some promising results

content.title: Interesting paper with some promising results
content.review:
Summary:

This paper addresses two major issues in previous works of long-tailed recognition: 1) models are over-confident on “head” classes. 2) the domain shift (dataset bias) is ignored in two-stage models. Accordingly, they propose two novel solutions including label-aware smoothing and shift learning on batch normalization. They also discover that mixup can improve the representation learning on long-tailed recognition. The experiments verify the effectiveness of their approaches and show the significant improvements on ImageNet-LT, iNaturalist, and Places-LT.

Pros:
- Overall, the presentation of this paper is clear and the writing is good.
- The authors address the issues in previous works and conduct various ablation studies for verification.
- The experimental results on benchmark datasets seem very promising and outperform baselines by a large margin.

Cons: 
- In experiments, I wonder if the authors apply mixup alone or with other basic augmentations, such as rotation, flipping. It would be interesting to see the performance combining with some basic augmentations since training without data augmentations usually gives bad performance.
- It would be nice to add a plot to indicate the difference among the three functions for eqn (3), e.g. move the left plot of figure 11 to the main text and explain their behaviors.

Overall, I find this paper interesting and novel.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer Feedback
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer's effort in reviewing our paper. We offer our responses to the reviewer’s questions and concerns as follows:

Q: mixup and augmentations.

A: In all our experiments, we apply mixup and other basic augmentations together. For CIFAR-LT's preprocessing, we mainly follow Cao et.al (https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.07413). For large scale datasets, e.g., ImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and iNaturalist 2018, our preprocessing mainly follows Kang et.al (https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09217). Moreover, we also find that applying additional augmentations such as CutMix (https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.04899) and AutoAugment (https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09501) can further improve accuracy performance. However, these calibration improvements are somewhat doubtful and limited.

We thank the nice suggestion that moving the left plot of Fig.11 to the main text and explaining their behaviors for better understanding. We will include these points in our revised vision.
